6. Surgicality and drafting quality

The analyses above measure how well models align with attorneys on substantive negotiation decisions. They do not capture whether the resulting document looks like a redline an attorney would actually send. Even a redline that addresses every substantive issue may be unsuitable for the counterparty if it effectively rewrites the agreement. We introduce surgicality to measure the precision of edits, examine differences in editing volume, and test how these behaviors relate to rubric scores.

6.1 Surgicality

Attorneys make most edits inline, while every model relies predominantly on block rewrites.

Every tracked-change event e in a deliverable is classified as inline or block. For an event in paragraph p, where a paired deletion and insertion at one anchor counts as one event, let de and ie be the characters it deletes and inserts, and up the characters of p outside any tracked change. τ is the inline threshold: an event counts as inline when its size, the larger of what it deletes and inserts, is less than τ times up.

size⁡(e)=max⁡(de,ie)(1)
inline⁡(e)={1ifsize⁡(e)<τ⋅up0otherwise,τ=0.30(2)
surgicality⁡(a)=1|C|∑c∈C1|Ea,c|∑e∈Ea,cinline⁡(e)(3)

Here C is the set of the 35 Turn 1 contracts and Ea,c the set of events in actor a's deliverables on contract c, so the surgicality score is the share of an actor's edits that are inline, averaged over the contracts. Redlined passages per task are the contiguous runs of paragraphs an actor touches in a deliverable. Edits per task are its events, inline and block. Edit volume is the sum of size⁡(e) over its events, in characters, and the typical insertion is the median insertion length.

We classify each tracked-change event as inline or block based on its size relative to the surrounding paragraph. An edit counts as inline when the larger of its insertion and deletion is less than 30% of the unchanged text in that paragraph. We then average the inline share across the 35 Turn 1 contracts.

Attorneys make 63.5% of their edits inline. Opus 5.5 leads the models at 36.6%, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 31.0%. The other five models range from 14.1% to 20.8%. Attorneys make most of their changes inline; every model makes most of its changes as block rewrites.

6.2 Editing volume

Attorneys cover similar ground through more frequent, smaller, and more targeted edits.

Table 11. Editing volume, attorneys versus models (mean and 95% CI)
MetricAttorneys, mean (95% CI)Models, mean (95% CI)
Redlined passages per task18.5 (15.9 to 21.2)19.0 (16.3 to 21.8)
Edits per task125 (102 to 148)41 (31 to 51)

Inline share63.5% (58.5% to 68.6%)22.0% (17.8% to 26.3%)
Edits per Turn 2 task63 (53 to 74)9 (8 to 10)

On Turn 1, attorneys and models redline almost the same number of passages per task, 18.5 versus 19.0, and change a similar amount of text overall, 10,675 versus 11,718 characters. The structure of those edits differs sharply. Attorneys make 125 tracked edits per task at an average length of 93 characters. Models make 41 edits at an average length of 300 characters.

Models therefore cover a similar document footprint with roughly one-third as many edits, each more than three times longer. On Turn 2, the gap widens further: attorneys make 63 tracked edits per task on average, compared with nine for models. That pattern matches the earlier Turn 2 results, where models score lower when responding to an existing redline.

6.3 Editing behavior and rubric reward

Redlining more passages loosely correlates with reward; longer edits do not.

Table 12. Correlation of rubric reward with editing behavior (Pearson r)
Turnr(reward, redlined passages)r(reward, insertion length)
Turn 1 (pooled over tasks)+0.29+0.14
Turn 2 (pooled over tasks)+0.23+0.05

The number of redlined passages has a modest positive relationship with rubric reward, at r = 0.29 on Turn 1 and r = 0.23 on Turn 2. Median insertion length shows little relationship, at r = 0.14 and r = 0.05. Models therefore gain more from identifying additional relevant issues than from making individual edits longer. This suggests the rubric taxonomy is robust to a simple reward-hacking strategy of inflating edits through large block rewrites.

7. Conclusion

Contract review is a judgment problem, and Ivo-micro1 ContractBench makes the judgment behind the markup measurable. Even the leading models satisfy fewer than 60% of weighted attorney-defined criteria on completed redlines. Models perform best when preserving acceptable language, but struggle with high-priority issues, positions that depend on the facts of the deal, and responding to counterparty redlines. GPT-6 Astra's strong performance on escalation criteria, despite its lower overall ranking, demonstrates why aggregate scores alone cannot capture the full range of model capabilities.

Attorneys redline with a scalpel, making frequent, small, inline edits; every model we tested relies predominantly on block rewrites. Ivo-micro1 ContractBench measures this difference through surgicality and editing volume, capturing a dimension of production readiness that substantive scores alone miss.

Ivo-micro1 ContractBench sets a standard that will outlast the models it currently ranks. It scores substance and style separately because attorneys still sit in the loop, and reporting the two apart tells practitioners where a model can be trusted and where it needs supervision. We also believe substantive judgment should remain the priority for post-training, and a leaderboard ranked on substance keeps that signal clean. The limitation is that such a leaderboard can reward the right positions reached through rewrites no attorney would send. A direction for Ivo-micro1 ContractBench v2 is to validate surgicality against attorney assessments of drafting quality and fold it into the overall leaderboard score, so that as models take on more of the redline end to end, the benchmark rewards a redline that is right on the substance and ready to send as written.
